questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=9-\frac{2}{3}x$ and the point $P(3,7)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(7).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(3,7).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =9-\frac{2}{3}x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{2}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(3,7)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(7,3)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(7) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(7))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{x+3}{5}$ and the point $P(2,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(2,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{x+3}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{5} \\ {f}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(2,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,2)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{2x+1}{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(4),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(4).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(4)=x.$ For $x\ne -1,$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(4) & =x \\ f(x) & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1} & =4 \\ \frac{2x+1}{x+1}\cdot (x+1) & =4\cdot (x+1) \\ \frac{2x+1}{\cancel{(x+1)}}\cdot \cancel{(x+1)} & =4x+4 \\ 2x+1 & =4x+4 \\ 2x & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(4)=-\frac{3}{2}.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x+1}{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2}) & =\frac{1}{{(-\frac{3}{2}+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(4) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(4))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function Using a Table
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=-1,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(-1)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-1))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(-1)=-2$ and ${f}^{′}(-2)=6.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
